alex: Hey - trying to repro a perf regression after the recent kernel-selection change. Latency spikes on long prompts, want to capture an nsys trace with CUDA kernels + NVTX ranges. Any recommended flags?

maya: Good call. For this kind of investigation I usually do full cuda + nvtx + osrt tracing and limit the capture window with NVTX ranges or duration. Example: 

```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-end=nvtx --output=alex_kv_spike -f --sample=cpu --duration=30s 
# then run the workload with NVTX push/pop around the request batch you want to profile
```

maya: The --sample=cpu helps reduce output size by sampling host stacks; if you need per-kernel timing set sampling off and capture full events (bigger file).

tom: If the regression only shows up under steady-state batching, wrap the steady-state section in NVTX so you don't capture startup/model-load overhead. Also you can `--capture-range=timer` for a wall-time slice. For very noisy runs, PID filter helps: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --pid=<PID>`

li: Heads up on file sizes: full cuda+osrt+nvt x for 30s -> GBs. If you see huge files, try: 
- smaller duration (5-10s)
- `--sample=cpu` or `--sample=none` depending on needs
- `--trace=cuda,nvtx` (drop osrt if you don't need OS runtime details)

li: Also consider `--capture-range=nvtx` + instrumenting our runtime around the KV cache lookup + batch flush logic so the trace focuses on the problematic path (KV miss -> load -> chunked kernels).

alex: Useful — how do we find kernel hotspots once we have the .nsys file?

maya: Open in Nsight Systems UI and check the GPU Kernel timeline first. Look for dense columns of tiny kernels (many launches) versus fewer large kernels. Tiny kernels per-token can kill throughput even if each kernel is fast. Use the Timeline -> GPU -> Top Functions view to sort by total GPU time.

maya: Also use the `nsys stats`/`nsys export` utilities to dump a summary: 

```
nsys export --format text --output summary.txt alex_kv_spike.qdrep
# or use `nsys stats alex_kv_spike.qdrep` for quick top-level metrics
```

tom: In past regressions we saw kernel-selection fallback creating many small GEMM calls because quantized-kernel fallback didn't vectorize batched sequence lengths. That shows as a lot of launch overhead on the timeline and idle gaps on the GPU. Check the Host thread swimlane for blocking syscalls around kernel launches too.

alex: Any tips for correlating NVTX ranges to kernel launches?

li: Name your NVTX ranges clearly, e.g., `nvtxRangePush("kv_lookup:prefix_len=128")`, and use color coding. Then in Nsight you can zoom an NVTX range and see exactly which kernels run inside it. If you use `--capture-range=nvtx` you can also limit to explicit push/pop region.

perf-bot: Suggestion: run with `--trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --capture-range=nvtx --output=run_alex_kv -f --quiet` and attach qdrep + sqlite export in the bug. Add `--force-overwrite` if re-running.

maya: If you need kernel source-level hotspots, enable `--trace=cuda` with `CUpti` collection and export to the sqlite database, then use `nsys stats -r cuda-kernels` to get per-kernel metrics (SM utilization, achieved occupancy). Low SM utilization + high launch rate usually points to many short kernels.

tom: For KV cache behavior specifically: instrument runtime to NVTX around cache hits vs misses. Miss path should show additional memcpy/host-side waits and then big GPU loads first followed by attention kernels. If you see many short memcpy + small kernel pairs, that's a batching policy problem.

alex: Are there pitfalls with sampling vs full trace that could hide the regression?

maya: Yes: sampling can miss short, frequent kernels because it captures stacks at intervals. Use full event tracing (no sampling) if you need exact kernel launch counts/timings. But only do that for very short durations or small runs. Sampling is good for narrow-down and for CPU stack hot spots.

li: Also watch out for clock scaling / power management affecting timings. Use `nvidia-smi -pm 1` and fix clocks for reproducible traces if possible.

tom: Quick command I use for a minimal high-fidelity capture of a 10s steady-state window: 

```
# instrument code with NVTX on the steady-state loop
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --output=minimal_kv_run -f --duration=10s
```

maya: After you open the qdrep, generate a kernel heatmap: Timeline -> GPU -> Kernel Launches -> right click -> Show Summary. That surfaces which kernels dominate time. Export the list of top kernels and cross-check against our kernel-selection log to see if the fallback kernels match.

alex: Great — I'll run a few short captures with NVTX around the suspect loop and attach the qdrep. If anyone can volunteer to look at the heatmap afterwards?

maya: I can take the first look. Please include the sqlite export too.

li: I'll script a wrapper to run 3 captures (5s each) with different batch sizes so we can compare kernel mix. Will post results here. :thumbsup:

perf-bot: Reminder: include model version, commit hash, runtime flags, and GPU model when filing the perf bug. That helps root-cause kernel selection differences.

alex: thanks folks, starting captures now.
